steps.text: Obalende, 6:47 p.m. The danfo hisses to a stop and Lagos hits you all at once: horns, plantain smoke, a conductor chanting destinations like a prayer.
Four years abroad. Nine days since Grandma Abeni was buried without you.
{name}!! Oya, come here! Four years and you still stand like somebody waiting for permission.

steps.prompt: Adaeze is already running toward you.

options.text: Drop your bag and hug her tight.
options.summary: You hugged Adaeze like no time had passed.

then.text: Okay, okay! People are looking. This is Obalende, not a Nollywood airport scene.

options.text: "You're late. Typical."
options.summary: You teased Adaeze the moment you saw her.

then.text: You're late. Typical.
Late? I have been here since the last time you ignored my calls. Carry your bag.

options.text: Glance at your phone. Barely look up.
options.summary: You barely looked up when Adaeze came to meet you.

then.text: Ah. So this is how it is.
She takes your bag anyway. That's the worst part.

steps.text: Mama Kudi's suya spot, off Awolowo Road. Same plastic stools. Same smoke. Same pepper that makes your eyes remember everything.
Two portions, Mama! Extra yaji! My friend has been eating foreign suya. That one is not suya, that is barbecue with an identity crisis.
I missed this. All of it. Even the pepper wahala.
{name}... before we eat. It's about Grandma's house.
Surveyors keep coming. Men with clipboards. And last week, somebody cut the padlock off the boat house.
{name}. Welcome home. I'm sorry about Grandma Abeni. Truly.
Tunde. Not tonight.
I came with respect. My father wants to make your family an offer for the property. A fair one. More than fair.
He slides a cream envelope across the table, right beside the suya.

options.text: Take the envelope. Hear him out.
options.summary: You took the Bakare family's envelope.

then.text: Leave it with me. I'll read it.
...Okay.

options.text: Push it back. "The house isn't for sale."
options.summary: You refused Tunde's offer on the spot.

then.text: The house isn't for sale. Not to you, not to your father.
You haven't even read it.

options.text: "Why is your father so desperate?"
options.summary: You wondered aloud why the Bakares want the house so badly.

then.text: Why is your father suddenly so desperate for a house nobody wanted last year?
Desperate? Nobody said desperate.

options.text: Let Adaeze stand with you.
options.lockedHint: You and Adaeze aren't close enough for this yet.
options.summary: Adaeze stood beside you against Tunde.

then.text: Adaeze shifts her stool beside yours, shoulder to shoulder. She doesn't say a word. She doesn't need to.
Two against one. Fine.

steps.text: Think it over. The offer expires at the end of the month.
The old house sits where the Lekki road gives up and turns into sand. NEPA has taken the light, as usual. A single lantern swings at the gate.
So you came. Eh-heh. I wasn't sure you would.
She left something for you, {name}. Only you. Not your father. Not Uncle Femi. Nobody.
Sade holds out a brass key, green with age, and a letter folded small.

steps.prompt: Grandma Abeni's last wish is in Sade's hands.

options.text: Take the key and the letter.

then.text: The key is heavier than it looks.

options.text: Take the letter only. "I'm not ready for the key."
options.summary: You left Grandma's key with Sade, for now.

then.text: Keep the key a little longer, Sade. I'm not ready.
She said you would say that.

steps.prompt: The letter trembles in your hand.

options.text: Read it now, by lantern light.
options.summary: You read Grandma Abeni's letter right away.

then.text: "My dear one. If you are reading this, the house still stands, and so do you."
"Do not sell. What your grandfather and old Chief Bakare buried behind the boat house in 1989 is not theirs to sell, and it is not yours to forget."
"Tell no Bakare. Trust Adaeze. — Abeni"
Whatever it says... I only carried it, okay?

options.text: Fold it away. Some truths can wait one more night.
options.summary: You decided to save the letter for later.

then.text: You slide the letter into your pocket. It feels like it's burning.

steps.text: Morning. Generator noise, sea breeze, and somebody banging on the gate like a debt collector.
Is this the famous {name}? I'm Zainab! I do events, music, and wahala. In that order.
Tonight: Sunset Sessions on the beach. Amapiano, jollof, a generator that has never failed me. And you, my dear, will be there.

steps.prompt: Zainab is not leaving without an answer.

options.text: "I'm in."
options.summary: You said yes to Zainab's beach party.

then.text: I'm in.
Beautiful! Wear something you can sweat in.

options.text: "I'm here to grieve, not to party."

then.text: I'm here to grieve, not to party.
I understand. But the sea doesn't judge. If you change your mind.

options.text: "Who else is going?"

then.text: Who else is going?
Everyone. Adaeze. Tunde and his people. And a few faces you won't expect.

steps.text: By sunset the beach has become a different country. Log drums, fairy lights, and the whole of Lekki pretending it has no problems.
Welcome to the only place in Lagos that never loses light. We have generator!
I told everyone you'd refuse that envelope. Zainab owes me five thousand naira.
So... you took the envelope. I'm not judging. I'm just... noticing.
You came! I was starting to think the sea swallowed you.

options.text: Dance with Adaeze
options.summary: You danced with Adaeze under the fairy lights.

then.text: Dance with me?
Ah! Okay, okay. But if you step on my foot, we are no longer friends.
For three songs, the whole city disappears.

options.text: Help Zainab when the speakers cut out
options.summary: You saved Zainab's set when the speakers died.

then.text: The music dies mid-beat. You find a loose cable behind the speaker stack and push it back in. The crowd roars.
You? On my equipment? ...Okay. You can stay.

options.text: Slip away to the shoreline
options.summary: You noticed a torch moving inside the boat house.

then.text: Past the lights, the sea is quiet. Down the beach, the boat house stands dark, except for a thin torch beam sliding behind its window.

steps.text: The music dips for half a second, the way it does when somebody important walks in.
A word, {name}. Alone.
Anything you say to {name}, you say in front of me.
I'll... be over there.

options.text: Follow Tunde to the dock.
options.summary: You heard Tunde out in private.

then.text: Smart. My father respects people who listen.
On the dock, Tunde triples the price. You can almost hear your grandmother laughing in the waves.

options.text: "Say it in front of Adaeze."
options.summary: You refused to talk behind Adaeze's back.

then.text: Whatever you want to say, say it in front of Adaeze.
...Fine. Another day.

options.text: "What did our grandfathers bury, Tunde?"
options.summary: You confronted Tunde about the secret behind the boat house.

then.text: What did our grandfathers bury behind that boat house, Tunde?
Who told you—
Buried? Buried what?

steps.text: Later, when the speakers finally rest, Adaeze walks you down the sand.
Adaeze trusts you. It shows in the way she lets her shoulder touch yours.
Whatever Grandma left you, whatever Tunde wants, you're not doing it alone. You hear me?
Adaeze keeps her distance. The sand between you feels wider than the sea.
I don't know if I know you anymore, {name}.
You stay in. The sea is loud tonight. So is the silence.
You didn't go to the party. Good. Sit. Let me tell you what Grandma never told your father.
Chief Bakare's father owed Grandma Abeni his life. She kept quiet for thirty years. Now the son wants the land.
Something is buried behind the boat house. I don't know what. I only know she checked that door every Sunday.
You didn't come to the party, so the party came to you.
She is carrying a foil pack of party jollof and two plastic spoons. You eat on the steps, laughing for the first time since you landed.
Wait. Is that a torch at the boat house?
The boat house leans over the water like it's listening. The padlock is gone. Only the blue door remains: paint peeling, salt-bitten, patient.
Hands shaking, you finally unfold Grandma's letter by torchlight. Do not sell. Tell no Bakare. Trust Adaeze.
So this is it? Whatever she was protecting?
The key turns on the second try. The door breathes out thirty years of stale air.
Inside: a rusted tin trunk. A ledger. Photographs. And one picture on top that makes Adaeze stop breathing.
That's my mother. With your grandmother. And old Chief Bakare. Why is my mother in this photo?
On the back, in Grandma Abeni's careful hand: "The three who kept the secret. Only two are left."
Adaeze... who's the third?
Headlights sweep across the water. A car door slams. Someone is walking toward the boat house, unhurried, like he owns the place.

steps.title: Episode 1 Complete
steps.text: You opened the door together. Whatever comes next, you won't face it alone.
I'll... stand guard out here. It's your family's secret, not mine.
The key turns. The door opens on darkness, salt, and the smell of old paper.
A tin trunk. A ledger. A photograph of three people: Grandma Abeni, Chief Bakare's father, and a woman whose face you almost recognize.
Your phone buzzes. An unknown number. One message: "Leave it. And don't trust her."

steps.title: Episode 1 Complete
steps.text: You opened the door alone. Now you wonder who was really standing behind it.
The padlock is gone, but there's a second lock beneath it. Brass. Old. And you don't have the key.
Maybe Sade still has it. We should go back.
Thank you for bringing us here, {name}. Some doors only open when the family is standing in front of them.
Two men with a locksmith's bag step out of the dark behind him.

steps.title: Episode 1 Complete
steps.text: Tunde got there first. The blue door won't stay closed for long.
